sources.title: The Alliance That Failed: Moscow and the Triple Alliance Negotiations, 1939
sources.citation: Roberts, G. (1996). 'The Alliance That Failed: Moscow and the Triple Alliance Negotiations, 1939.' European History Quarterly, 26(3), pp. 383-414.
sources.supported_claim: British and French military delegations were sent to Moscow by slow merchant ship, arrived without full negotiating powers, and Voroshilov's August 14 question about Polish/Romanian transit rights went unanswered by the Western side, precipitating the talks' collapse.

sources.title: The Soviet Union and the Origins of the Second World War: Russo-German Relations and the Road to War, 1933-1941
sources.citation: Roberts, G. (1995). The Soviet Union and the Origins of the Second World War: Russo-German Relations and the Road to War, 1933-1941. Macmillan.
sources.supported_claim: Analytical framing of the August 1939 pact as a pragmatic Soviet response to the failure of collective-security diplomacy with Britain and France, intended to secure a buffer and time for rearmament rather than as ideological alignment with Germany.

sources.title: Telegram from Ambassador Laurence A. Steinhardt to the Secretary of State, August 23, 1939
sources.author_or_institution: United States Department of State, Foreign Relations of the United States, 1939, Volume I
sources.supported_claim: Contemporaneous diplomatic reporting, the same day the pact was signed, that Poland's refusal to accept Soviet military assistance was the acknowledged cause of the Anglo-Franco-Soviet talks' failure, and that a Soviet-German agreement was already understood as imminent.

sources.title: Secret Additional Protocol to the Treaty of Nonaggression Between Germany and the U.S.S.R.
sources.author_or_institution: The Avalon Project, Yale Law School (hosting the German Foreign Office/Nuremberg document text)
sources.date: Signed August 23, 1939; hosted document, ongoing archive
sources.supported_claim: Full text of the secret protocol assigning Finland, Estonia, Latvia, and Bessarabia to the Soviet sphere of influence and setting the Narew-Vistula-San line as the German-Soviet demarcation in Poland.

sources.title: Memorandum by Karl Schnurre on the German-Soviet Credit Agreement of August 19, 1939
sources.author_or_institution: The Avalon Project, Yale Law School (German Foreign Office document)
sources.date: Memorandum dated August 29, 1939, describing the August 19, 1939 agreement
sources.supported_claim: Terms of the German-Soviet commercial credit agreement (200 million Reichsmarks) signed August 19, 1939, four days before the non-aggression pact, and its role as an economic precursor to the political agreement.

sources.title: Nomonhan, 1939: The Red Army's Victory That Shaped World War II
sources.citation: Goldman, S. D. (2012). Nomonhan, 1939: The Red Army's Victory That Shaped World War II. Naval Institute Press.
sources.supported_claim: Scale and timing of the Khalkhin Gol (Nomonhan) undeclared border war between Soviet and Japanese forces, including Zhukov's decisive August 20-31, 1939 offensive, as a live two-front consideration for Soviet decision-makers in August 1939.

sources.title: The Forgotten Soviet-Japanese War of 1939
sources.supported_claim: Corroborating summary of Khalkhin Gol's scale, timing, and its overlap with the German-Soviet pact negotiations, and Japan's shocked reaction to the pact's announcement.

sources.title: German-Soviet Pact
sources.author_or_institution: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, Holocaust Encyclopedia
sources.supported_claim: General chronology cross-check of the pact's signature, secret protocol terms, and its collapse with the German invasion of the USSR on June 22, 1941.

sources.title: German-Soviet Nonaggression Pact
sources.supported_claim: General chronology cross-check: signing date and negotiators, ten-year term of the pact, and its role in enabling the German invasion of Poland.

sources.title: What Stalin Knew: The Enigma of Barbarossa
sources.citation: Murphy, D. E. (2005). What Stalin Knew: The Enigma of Barbarossa. Yale University Press.
sources.supported_claim: Documentation of the extensive intelligence warnings Stalin received before June 22, 1941 and his refusal to act on them, supporting the outcome-quality assessment that the additional time bought by the pact was not used to prepare for the eventual German invasion.
